newsitem.title: THAILAND: Burma blast raises fears of fresh violence.
newsitem.headline: Burma blast raises fears of fresh violence.

text.p: Questions remain over who masterminded Sunday's deadly bomb blast in Burma, but one thing is certain -- the attack adds a new element of violence to an already tense political situation, analysts said on Tuesday.
"This is a new, most unwelcome development in Burma's political culture," said a Rangoon-based diplomat.
"They do a lot of nasty things to each other, but parcel bombs are a whole different issue," he said. "This is not something traditionally part of the political culture here."
An explosion, thought to have been caused by a parcel bomb, ripped through the house of Lieutenant-General Tin Oo on Sunday evening, killing his eldest daughter, Cho Lei Oo.
Tin Oo is one of the four most powerful men in the government and is Secretary Two of the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC).

Burma's military government, already fraught with international image problems and simmering domestic unrest, said in a statement late on Tuesday that the attack was masterminded by anti-government groups based in Japan.
"Initial investigation revealed that the terrorist bomb that exploded at Lieutenant-General Tin Oo's residence on the evening of 6 April 1997 was airmailed from Japan," the statement said.
"There are reasons to believe that the bomb plot was masterminded by some anti-Myanmar (Burma) government groups within Japan which have resorted to acts of terrorism."

There are several active exile groups in Japan and other Asian countries such as Thailand and India. Exiled groups in Thailand have been blamed for previous bomb attacks in Burma but all have denied involvement in Sunday's explosion.

The blast followed a bombing last December, which killed five people and wounded 17, at a Buddhist shrine in Rangoon. The government blamed that attack on the Karen National Union (KNU) ethnic guerrilla group.
Diplomats said parcel bombs are not a typical tactic used by Burma's rebel groups, which are more adept at jungle warfare than urban guerrilla violence.
"It's one thing to toss a grenade, but another thing to organise a mail bomb," one Rangoon diplomat said. "You have to look at the capabilities of those suspected."
However, in early March the KNU -- which was being fiercely attacked on the border by Burmese troops -- threatened heightened guerrilla activity within Burma.
Some diplomats also said Sunday's bombing could have been orchestrated by someone within the government and could be a sign of a split in the SLORC.
It appears to be the second attempt against Tin Oo, who was the last senior official to visit the sacred Tooth Relic Pagoda in Rangoon before it was bombed on Christmas day.
Tin Oo is a hardliner within the SLORC, and as Army Chief of Staff has given many speeches to troops urging them to "annihilate" anyone who disrupts the stability of the state.
The bombing is the latest in a series of problems for Burma's military government, which has been grappling to control religious unrest since mid-March.
December's shrine blast sparked fears of an urban guerrilla movement.
Diplomats had said at the time the people responsible for that bombing might have been taking advantage of rare student unrest earlier in the month.
In the same vein, the latest attack could be seen as an opportunity to take advantage of the uncertainty caused by two weeks of unrest between Buddhists and Moslems across the country, analysts said.
The religious unrest led the government to impose curfews and other restrictions in various cities.
Diplomats said security would be tight over the next few weeks, especially leading up to and during the "Thingyan" traditional water festival from April 13 to 17.

The festival, which consists of people dousing each other with water and holding parties in the streets, is usually the only time during the year that Burmese are allowed to gather together in the streets.
"I think they are very concerned about security," said one Asian diplomat. "And there are rumours of other things going on and possible disturbances that might take place next week."
